analysis.one_liner: Makes employers face large fines and up to 20 years in prison when willful safety violations kill workers.
analysis.headline: A bill to raise criminal penalties for employers whose willful safety violations kill workers was sent to the Senate labor committee in April 2005 and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the law as it stood, an employer who willfully violated a safety rule and killed a worker faced at most a $10,000 fine and six months in prison for a first offense. This bill would replace those caps with the standard criminal fine schedule used in federal felony cases and prison terms of up to 10 years for a first offense and 20 years for repeat offenses. It would also raise penalties for giving inspectors false information or tipping them off before an inspection. The bill was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in hazardous jobs and the families of workers killed on the job. The point is deterrence: when an employer weighs ignoring a known safety hazard, the personal risk to its executives would no longer be a fine smaller than the cost of fixing the problem. Honest employers who already invest in safety would also face less undercutting by competitors that cut corners.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and families of employees killed on the job

how_it_helps.text: Raises the maximum prison term for a willful safety violation that kills a worker from six months to 10 years, and from one year to 20 years for a second conviction.
Replaces fixed caps of $10,000 and $20,000 with the standard federal criminal fine schedule, which allows fines scaled to the seriousness of the offense and the offender's gain.
Raises penalties for knowingly giving false information to OSHA and for unauthorized advance notice of an inspection, from small fines and six months to up to two years in prison.

analysis.who_pays: Employers whose willful safety violations kill or endanger workers would face far greater fines and the possibility of prison for responsible individuals. That cost falls on rule-breaking firms, not on companies that follow the law.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers who willfully violate safety rules

drawbacks.text: Raising criminal penalties does not add a single workplace inspection, and under the existing system OSHA inspects only a small fraction of workplaces each year, so the new penalties would rarely be charged unless enforcement also grew.

Critics of tougher workplace criminal liability argue that criminal charges for industrial accidents can punish genuine accidents and make companies more defensive in cooperating with investigators, since proving that a violation was 'willful' is difficult and contested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real gap: the maximum criminal penalty for a willful violation that kills a worker was a $10,000 fine and six months in prison, a sum many firms would treat as a routine cost of doing business. Higher penalties and prison exposure are a plausible deterrent, though the bill's weakness is that penalties alone, without more inspections and stronger prosecution, would apply only in the rare cases that get charged. The costs fall on employers who willfully break safety law, which most people would consider the right party to bear them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on April 28, 2005, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Corzine introduced the Workplace Wrongful Death Accountability Act on April 28, 2005, with Sens. Kennedy, Lautenberg, and Durbin as cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No further action was taken; the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that willfully violate safety rules are better off, because the threat of meaningful fines and prison terms for killings on the job was never created. Workers and their families gained nothing from a bill that never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that break safety rules; no one else

for.name: Sen. Jon Corzine
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise criminal penalties for willful OSHA violations that kill workers.

for.name: Sens. Edward Kennedy, Frank Lautenberg, and Richard Durbin

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it received no hearing or vote in the 109th Congress.

against.name: Sen. Mike Enzi
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republicans signed on; the bill then died in a committee chaired by a Republican without any recorded opposition votes.

industries.industry: Employers in high-hazard industries (construction, manufacturing, meatpacking, mining)
industries.note: The bill would expose these firms to federal felony-level fines and prison terms of up to 10 years for a first offense when willful safety violations kill workers. Its defeat left the existing maximum in place: a $10,000 fine and six months in prison for a first offense, sums small enough to be treated as a business cost.

Not an industry but the bill's intended beneficiaries: it would have created real criminal accountability for deaths caused by willful safety violations. Its death in committee left them with no new remedy.
